abstract: Can Newton's live MCP harness be tuned until agents set up and tune simulations more efficiently with it than without it? This page tracks an ongoing improvement loop on tasks drawn from earlier reports: tuning a humanoid tracking controller, fixing a grasp that slips, and calibrating models against real-robot data (a DFKI double pendulum and, from iteration 3, 570 real cube tosses). Each iteration runs Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra in concurrent pairs; the same agent solves the same task either with the live MCP or by editing and rerunning scripts, and every submission is verified in a fresh process. The transcripts are then mined for friction, and the harness is changed. After three iterations (14 pairs), both conditions have solved every task, and the harness changes have moved the MCP's efficiency in opposite directions for the two agents. For GPT-6 Astra, iteration 2 turned the MCP from a cost (1.38× input tokens, 1.24× time in iteration 1) into a clear saving (0.57× tokens, 0.69× time on three tasks). For Opus, the MCP stayed faster over all pairs (time 0.85×) but used more tokens (1.29×); an iteration-2 setting that disabled tool search doubled Opus's first-turn context from 15k to 30k tokens. The loop also found and fixed three ways a live session could silently diverge from the script. Resets reverted the agent's own settings. Quick edits could reload stale bytecode. And the iteration-1 automatic CUDA-graph recapture, applied around the same MuJoCo solver, corrupted memory: in iteration 2 a grasped cube fell through the table and one session crashed. A one-box reproduction traces this to solver buffers that are first allocated inside a captured step. Iteration 3, now running, recaptures only for replaced solvers, restores Opus's context size, and adds the cube-toss task.
loop: The previous study showed that a live MCP makes photo-based calibration cheaper in tokens. This loop asks a broader question. Can the harness be tuned until it reliably helps on the setup and tuning work that earlier coding agents often failed at? The three tasks are rebuilt from earlier reports. One tunes a controller for reference-motion following (from the G1 whole-body-control report). One debugs a slipping grasp (from grasp-shake-drift and FeatherPGS). One calibrates a model against measurements from a real robot.

Each task starts from a runnable Newton example script with a realistic defect, together with a goal checked by a hidden verifier. The same agent (Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code, or GPT-6 Astra in Codex, both at xhigh effort) receives the same task in two conditions. In the MCP condition the script is already running live under python -m newton.mcp host. The agent can execute Python inside it, observe it, and reload the edited file, and it keeps its shell. In the no-MCP baseline it edits files and reruns scripts, so every run starts a fresh simulator process. Both trials of a pair start together on the same machine and get a 30-minute budget.

One iteration runs the pairs, reads the transcripts for friction (wasted turns, errors, source-code spelunking, redundant checks), and changes the harness. The change is committed as a new harness version, and the next iteration reruns the pairs. We report success, elapsed time (split into model and tool time), input and output tokens, API cost, and tool calls. Paired ratios below 1 favor the MCP.
task_rows: Franka FR3 grasps a 4 cm cube and shakes it (scene from the grasp-shake-drift report). A robot-wide soft contact default (ke = 250) is imposed on the cube through the fingers' higher MuJoCo geom priority, so a 10 cm shake drops the cube.
Cube drift in the hand frame below 1 mm over 11.5 s of 3 cm shaking and below 5 mm over 6 s of 10 cm shaking. Motion, gains, grip, timestep, and cube are unchanged.
Unitree G1 (29 DoF, SolverMuJoCo) follows a Kimodo wave clip with joint PD servos at 10 Hz bandwidth and falls within about a second.

Robot stays upright, with root RMSE ≤ 4 cm and joint RMSE ≤ 0.05 rad on the clip and on an unseen 1.4× faster playback. No forces on the floating base; robot model unchanged. A harder clip (high5) is reported but not required.
Identify a system from real data

Model of the DFKI torque-controlled double pendulum (design C.0) built from nominal CAD point masses without friction, armature, or damping. Ten real recordings (measured joint angles, velocities, and motor torques at about 500 Hz) are provided.

Multiple-shooting error on two held-out recordings, using 0.5 s open-loop windows started from measured states and driven by measured torques. It must be ≤ 0.060 rad on a 20 s excitation run and ≤ 0.150 rad on a 75 s run with full swings.
Identify contact parameters from real data

A 0.1048 m, 0.37 kg acrylic cube tossed onto a wooden table (ContactNets dataset, 148 Hz tracking). The starter uses untuned contact settings (μ = 0.5, ke = 2.5 kN/m, kd = 100 N·s/m). 400 real tosses are provided, one Newton world per toss.

Open-loop rollout of 170 held-out tosses from their first frame. Mean time-averaged position error must be ≤ 0.020 m and orientation error ≤ 0.45 rad. Cube size, mass, inertia, and gravity are unchanged.
results: Every trial so far solved its task in both conditions, so efficiency, not success, separates the conditions. Over all 14 completed pairs, the MCP reduced elapsed time (geometric-mean ratio 0.88, 95% interval 0.73–1.05) at about equal input tokens (1.10, 0.87–1.36) and API cost (1.05, Claude Code only).

The per-agent split is more informative. GPT-6 Astra was slower and costlier with the h1 harness (time 1.24×, input tokens 1.38×). With h2 it was faster and cheaper on all three tasks (time 0.69×, interval 0.54–0.84; tokens 0.57×, 0.48–0.75). On G1 tracking it took 326 s and 0.53M tokens instead of 598 s and 1.0M; on grasp drift, 235 s and 0.58M tokens instead of 332 s and 1.2M. Opus finished faster with the MCP in every iteration (time 0.71× with h1), but its token ratio rose from 1.03× with h1 to 1.63× with h2. The cause is traced in Section 3: h2 disabled Claude Code's tool search to load the Newton tools up front, which also loaded every built-in tool schema and doubled the first-turn context.
Iteration 3 (harness h3) is running on four tasks, including the new cube-toss calibration, with second replicates for Opus. Its pairs will appear here as they complete.
harness: Each version is a commit on the Newton branch eric-heiden/newton-live-mcp, driven by what the previous iteration's transcripts showed.

h0 → h1. Iteration-0 agents wrote the same frame-by-frame evaluation loops in almost every call. They grepped the MuJoCo solver source to learn which contact parameters were in effect, and a missing import newton invalidated the scene. h1 added rollout(), solver_contacts(), health(), a preloaded newton, and non-invalidating errors for hosted scripts. It also added automatic CUDA-graph recapture after live attribute edits, and compiling reloaded scripts from source; a regression test had shown that a script edited within the same second could reload stale bytecode. Correction: an earlier version of this page said an iteration-0 agent's live shake-amplitude edit was silently ignored because it was baked into a captured graph. That was wrong: the example passes the amplitude to a kernel launched outside its graphs, so the edit took effect.

h1 → h2. In iteration 1, Astra's first call to solver_contacts() found the grasp's root cause directly: the fingers' higher geom priority imposes a soft material with a 0.2 s solref time constant on the cube. Opus still read solver source for the same fact; in h1 the helper was listed only in the server instructions, not in the task's host guide. MCP tool results were smaller than the no-MCP shell output (72k vs 110k characters on grasp drift), so the token overhead had to come from elsewhere. It came from about 2.4k tokens of tool schemas and instructions resent on every turn, and from about 10% more turns. h2 advertises only newton_execute and newton_rebuild with short instructions (about 0.8k tokens), names the deciding material in the contact report, lists the helpers in the host guide, and hosts two worker copies of the scene for parallel or background sweeps. To skip the tool-search round trip, it also set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false.

h2 → h3. Iteration 2 exposed three problems. (1) ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false loads the schemas of every deferred built-in Claude Code tool, not just Newton's: Opus MCP trials started at 30k tokens instead of 15k. h3 marks only the Newton server alwaysLoad, which gives 14.9k with no tool-search round trip. (2) Checkpoints and resets restored every scalar attribute of the hosted example, so a look-ahead or gain the agent set before rollout(start=True) was silently reverted, and one sweep returned identical rows. h3 rewinds only the scalars that step() itself advances. (3) An Opus grasp session crashed with CUDA error 700 after live solver experiments. Reproducing it showed that h1's recapture was unsafe. Newton examples capture a graph around the solver's first step, and SolverMuJoCo allocates buffers during that step, so those buffers belong to the first graph. Recording a second graph around the same solver either segfaults or silently corrupts the simulation (a grasped cube ended 99 m below the table). A one-box scene fails the same way, and one eager step before the first capture avoids it. h3 recaptures only when example.solver has been replaced, which is safe. For other changes it reports that values inside the captured graphs keep their old values until a rebuild. recapture() refuses to run around the same solver. The grasp and G1 MCP trials of iterations 1 and 2 hit such recaptures (for example 10 times in the i2 Opus grasp trial). Their live numbers may have been corrupted, although their verified submissions were not affected.
harness_rows: ExampleHost serves an unmodified example script live. Checkpoints include the example's own arrays and scalars, and rebuild reloads the script in-process. Code profile with five tools.

rollout(), solver_contacts(), and health() helpers; newton preloaded; Python errors keep hosted scenes valid; automatic CUDA-graph recapture after live attribute edits (unsafe, see h3); quiet Warp logs; rebuild compiles from source.

Lean profile (execute + rebuild; per-turn schema and instructions about 0.8k instead of 2.4k tokens); ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false (regression for Claude Code); contact report names the deciding material; two worker copies for parallel and background sweeps; zero-argument rollout probes.

Newton server alwaysLoad instead of disabling tool search; resets keep agent-assigned settings; graph recapture only for replaced solvers, with notes for changes that cannot reach captured graphs; cube-toss task.
real: The system-identification task uses public measurements from the DFKI underactuated double pendulum (BSD-3-Clause). The robot has two quasi-direct-drive AK80-6 motors with 6:1 gearing, a 0.2 m first link, and a 0.3 m second link. Its fourteen design C.0 system-identification runs record measured joint angles, velocities, and motor torques. Runs 00–09 are given to the agent, while runs 10 (20 s excitation) and 11 (75 s, full swings, 300 Hz) are held out. The model replicates one pendulum per evaluation window as a separate Newton world, so a whole recording is evaluated in one batched SolverMuJoCo rollout (about 0.5 s on the study GPU).

The thresholds were set before any agent trial, from three reference parameter sets. The nominal starter misses badly. The published DFKI identification, mapped to a physically valid Newton model, roughly halves the error but does not pass. A direct Nelder–Mead fit of all twelve Newton parameters to runs 07–09 passes with margin. So the gates reward calibrating the simulator itself, beyond copying published numbers.

The agents solved this task quickly and in the same way in both conditions. They fitted the identifiable base parameters by linear least squares on inverse dynamics, then refined them with their own NumPy (Opus) or C++ (Astra) forward models under the multiple-shooting objective, and used Newton only to confirm. On a two-link system the simulator is not needed in the inner loop, so the live MCP has little to offer here. Its value should show on systems where the simulator is the only practical forward model, with contact or many degrees of freedom.
dp_reference_rows: DFKI published identification (model 3.0, mapped to Newton)
findings: Frontier agents now solve these setup and tuning tasks with or without the MCP. All 28 verified trials passed, so the harness has to earn its place through efficiency and reliability.

Harness details decide whether the MCP saves or costs tokens. The same MCP ranged from 1.38× to 0.57× input tokens for Astra, and from 1.03× to 1.63× for Opus, depending on how tools are advertised and loaded. Per-turn fixed context (schemas and instructions resent on every call) and extra turns account for the overhead, not tool output. The last knob moved the wrong way for Opus, because it disabled deferral for all built-in tools too.

The MCP saves wall-clock time most reliably when fresh runs are expensive. Opus was faster with the MCP in every iteration (0.85× overall), most on G1 tracking and grasp drift. On the two-link pendulum, fresh processes are cheap and both agents fitted parameters with their own NumPy or C++ models, so the MCP added little.

A live session needs guards that a restart workflow gets for free. Three silent-divergence bugs surfaced only through agent use: settings reverted by reset, stale bytecode after a quick edit, and memory corruption from recapturing a CUDA graph around a warm solver. A live harness is only as trustworthy as its bookkeeping, and each fix has a regression test.

The MuJoCo capture issue is a Newton bug worth fixing at the source. Capturing a CUDA graph around a new SolverMuJoCo leaves buffers allocated inside that graph, and a second capture around the same solver crashes, on upstream Newton main as well (repro linked in Section 7). Examples that warm up with one eager step before capturing avoid it.

Explaining effective solver parameters saves investigation. Where an agent used the contact report, it found the grasp's root cause (finger priority overriding the cube's material) in its first call. Agents without it read solver kernels to reconstruct the same fact.
limits: This is an exploratory loop, not a registered study. The harness changes between iterations, three pairs per agent and iteration cannot separate small effects from noise, and tasks are added as the loop goes. All pairs ran on one shared 4-CPU machine with a MIG GPU slice. Concurrent pairs control for load between conditions but not across iterations, and reference fits sometimes ran during trials.

Iteration 0 has no Astra trials. One iteration-1 Astra G1 pair was excluded because the operator accidentally terminated its live host while testing workers; it was rerun with the same harness. Live results in some iteration-1 and iteration-2 MCP trials may have been corrupted by the recapture bug described in Section 3; their verified submissions were not. Codex does not report API cost. Because every task so far is solvable in both conditions, these results say nothing yet about whether the MCP raises success on harder problems.
source: Newton branch eric-heiden/newton-live-mcp: the MCP host and helpers are in newton/_src/mcp, and the loop harness, tasks, and verifiers in tools/mcp_evaluation/v4 (run_v4.py; dp_real/prepare_data.py and cube_toss/prepare_data.py rebuild the data files from the public datasets). Trial data: loop.json (every trial's metrics and paired ratios) and loop-transcripts.zip (prompts, specs, summaries, verifications, submitted scripts, agent transcripts, and host logs, with loopback tokens redacted). CUDA-graph recapture repro: mujoco_recapture_repro.py.
real_cube: From iteration 3 a second real dataset is used where the simulator is the practical forward model: the ContactNets cube tosses (BSD-3-Clause), 570 hand tosses of an acrylic cube onto a wooden table tracked at 148 Hz (Pfrommer et al., CoRL 2020). The cube's size, mass, and inertia are measured and fixed. The agent calibrates contact behavior (friction, stiffness, damping, torsional friction, table height, solver settings) so that open-loop rollouts from each toss's first frame reproduce the recorded bounces, slides, and tumbles. Each toss is one Newton world, and a CUDA-graph rollout of all 400 training tosses takes about 2–4 s.

The thresholds were set before any agent trial. Published parameters do not transfer. The ContactNets friction coefficient with untuned stiffness halves the position error but leaves orientation unchanged. The MuJoCo fit of Acosta et al., mapped to Newton's contact model, is worse than friction alone, because stiffness and damping mean different things across simulators and timesteps. A Nelder–Mead fit of five Newton contact parameters on 200 training tosses passes with margin.
